nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, critic, essayist and lawyer of Boston and Cambridge, the elder Richard Henry Dana, father of Richard Henry Dana the younger (1815-1882) the writer of the seagoing narrative Two Years Before the Mast, to which this record does not belong
literary_identity: A writer of romantic narrative verse, of a few short lyrics, of a prose romance fragment and of criticism and editorial matter, joined to a long career as a lawyer and as a man of letters. This record covers the father: the poet and critic of 1815 to 1840 and the conservative man of letters of the later Cambridge years. His son, of the same name, wrote the prose narrative of the California coast and the legal and political works of the 1860s and 1870s, and the two are constantly confounded in short accounts and in library catalogues.
biography: He was born at Cambridge in Massachusetts on 15 November 1787 into the old Dana family of that town, descended from the Cambridge settler of 1640 and allied to the leading families of the coast, a connection which gave him its manners and its politics. He was entered at Harvard as a boy, studied there through several terms and quitted the College in 1807 without a degree, removing to the law, in which he was admitted and in which he afterwards practised at Boston with fair success and with small appetite for the work. About 1815 he was one of the young men who founded the North American Review, the quarterly which gave Boston the command of American criticism for a generation, and to which he contributed some of the earliest and most discussed of its papers. In 1821 and 1822 he conducted The Idle Man, a monthly of sketches and essays in the manner of the Spectator which ran to six numbers and which he chiefly wrote; it was the most notable of the many rivals of Irving's Sketch Book, and the failure of its subscriptions taught him the narrowness of the American book trade. In 1827 he published the volume of Poems which contained his reputation and the long narrative The Buccaneer, a tale of the sea and of the rover of the Spanish main, with the prose romance Paul Felton and other pieces of his earlier years; the poem was praised in Edinburgh by the critic who wrote as Christopher North, and gave him the place of the accomplished and melancholy poet of the Boston school. Through the following decades he wrote little and published less, living at Cambridge as a lawyer, a critic and a consulted man of letters, an unrepentant conservative in politics and in taste, and an authority upon the older literature of New England. He survived his generation, his friends and his reputation, and died at his house in Boston on 2 February 1879 in his ninety-second year; his son had preceded him into print with the book that has since kept the name of Dana before readers, and the two are still so constantly confounded that the elder's verse is seldom read without a correction of the biography.
literary_profile: His printed work is small and was collected late: the Poems of 1827, which gathered the narrative verse and the lyrics written from his student years onward, the prose fragment Paul Felton, the sketches and essays of The Idle Man of 1821 and 1822, and the reviews and articles contributed to the North American Review and to the magazines of the 1810s and 1820s. The verse is romantic and narrative in the English manner, dealing with the sea, with guilt and with the return to settlement, and the shorter pieces, of which The Little Beach Bird is the best known, are lyric in the eighteenth-century sense rather than in the Wordsworthian. His prose criticism, and the essays of the Idle Man, are the part of his work which the history of the American essay has kept.
stylistic_characteristics: A dignified, deliberate and deliberately old-fashioned blank verse, sound in ear but not various, with long descriptive sweeps of sea and coast and a moral weight laid upon the closing lines; in the prose an eighteenth-century periodic sentence, ironic, restrained and formal, carrying the manner of the periodical essay into American subject. He is at home in the narrative of guilt and retribution and in the elevated description, and uneasy in rapid dialogue and in comedy; his diction keeps the vocabulary of the older English poetry and avoids the colloquial.
intellectual_concerns: The guilt and the retribution of the passionate and solitary man; the sea as a scene of moral discipline and of doom; the culture of the mind and the refinement of taste as the end of letters; the claims of the old conservative order in a democratic country; the dignity and the perils of the literary profession in America, where the magazine and the subscription list governed what could be written; the distinction of masculine and feminine powers in writing, which he argued; the duty of criticism and the memory of the New England past.
historical_significance: He was one of the founders of the North American Review, the organ through which Boston dominated American criticism for a generation, and the editor and chief writer of The Idle Man, the most accomplished American attempt at the periodical essay of the 1820s. The Buccaneer gave American romantic narrative verse one of its serious specimens and won him a British notice of consequence, and his essays and reviews set the standard of taste against which the native subject of the sea and of the New England town was judged. He is also of consequence as the father of the author of Two Years Before the Mast and as the instance most cited of the elder generation of Boston men of letters who could live by the law and by criticism but not by poetry alone.
major_influences: The English romantic narrative and the tale of guilt and retribution in the manner of the later Byron and of the ballad school
the periodical essay of Addison and Goldsmith as read in the Harvard and Boston libraries
the sea stories and the pirate histories of the Atlantic
Coleridge and the English lyric of conversation in his shorter verse
the Edinburgh and London review criticism which he imitated in the North American Review
the Cambridge and Boston family tradition of New England letters and of Federalist politics
biographical_uncertainty: The day and month of his death are reported variously in the printed records, one archive finding aid placing it in July 1879 while the biographical accounts give 2 February of that year; the extent of his share in the founding and in the early numbers of the North American Review, and the division of authorship among the several conductors of that journal, have never been settled. The reason for his withdrawal from Harvard without a degree is reported from family and later biographical accounts rather than from the College record, and the claim that he supplied the preface to his son's narrative of 1840 rests upon the memoirs of the family rather than upon a documented statement of authorship.
